text:
So guys, we wanted to thank you all  of your comments on this video.  We are in the process of setting up additional tests with AIB GTX 1080 Ti cards.  They should arrive Friday or Monday thanks to the slow shipping here in Canada & the prices have been logged for reference.  The intent is to see how a downdraft cooler affects the GTX 1080 Ti's performance results and judge performance per dollar accordingly.  :)

We insured that the AIB cards ordered weren't top-shelf products like the STRIX OC or AMP Extreme as those represent the highest-spec GTX 1080 Ti cards around and they still cost $800+ at most retailers.  Comparing to those would artificially skew results negatively for the 1080 Ti both positively and negatively.  

As usual, we ALWAYS test the closest thing possible to a "reference" version at launch.  That hasn't changed in the last 14 years of HWC on the website and here on Youtube, nor will it change.  Over the last half decade the entire point of insuring our graphics cards are tested the way they are is to replicate (as accurately as possible that is) real world gaming results and that means longer-duration load scenarios.  This was originally done because NVIDIA and AMD GPUs can obscure poor overall performance by featuring extremely high clock speeds in the first 30 seconds to minute of testing.  After that point the GPU core heats up and clock speeds are dynamically lowered.  In this case it resulted in both Founders Editions behaving in the way they did.  We feel this is a more realistic way to test but and in this case it may have shown why blower-style cards (Founders and AIB versions) can be inferior choices in some cases.

text:
Going to pin this comment since there seems to be a lot of interesting feedback. First and foremost, due to the nature of hardware benchmarking, different scenes being used, settings, different games, variable hardware configurations and more, comparing one publication's results to another's is utterly pointless.  

A good example is the way we start off the benchmarking sequence.  This was mentioned in the video and it's a KEY element of our methodologies, which a lot of folks are missing.  We let EVERY card "warm up" under load for 2 minutes before starting a benchmark run. This gives stability to the results. If you just jump from one game to another, the card has time to cool off before beginning the next run.  Yeah it takes more time but it gives us (IMO) a more accurate picture of in-game results. 

While there's no way to validate it, this can have a pretty big impact upon the RTX 2080 vs GTX 1080Ti results since the RTX drops just 65MHz after two minutes or so, the GTX 1080 Ti Founders Edition drops about 185MHz from its top-end Boost Clock.  Validation here:  http://bit.ly/2PQCL9N

Anyways, there's a lot more to be taken into account here but if you haven't watched every second of the video, you would have missed this key piece of information.
